https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ev: Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee Jones
"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.
The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.
A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.
About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.
The BBC saw mould on ceilings and overflowing rubbish when we visited Castleview House

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support .

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.
Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".
The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.
Promotional materials such as this social media post advertise the homes as "Secure, Government-Backed Wealth"
Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6eq: Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature

A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.
Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.
France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies .

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.
In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.
Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.
The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.
As Europe sees a wave of cyber-attacks on commercial fridges, we investigate how everyday devices are vulnerable to basic attacks using easily-available tools.
The security threat was discovered by staff at refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.
They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.
"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.
There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:
In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted
On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted
On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted
The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).
RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.
As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0: Sean Cairncross (left) was appointed by the Trump administration
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired after losing the confidence of the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, according CBS, the BBC's US news partner. Asked about his removal on Friday, President Donald Trump said it was because he was not "good enough".
His firing comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.
US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.

There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X , external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The news, first reported by Axios , external , follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.
Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.
In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.
He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.
While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.
The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent , or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.
Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.
It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.
The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.
Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.
Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.
The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.
But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.
AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.
It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.
One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.
The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.
And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.
It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.
Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.
It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.
In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses
Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI .
It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.
The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.

In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument , external around smart glasses.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674: Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.
Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.
The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.
Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.
The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.
But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.
But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.
Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.
The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.
While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.
Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.
Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.
The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z7: After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.
There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews. , external
Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.
GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.
Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating , external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".
One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.
The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.
It's the game that shocked and thrilled the world: Grand Theft Auto. As a new installment is released in 2026, go deep into the history of the game with rapper Bugzy Malone.
The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".
It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.
"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.
Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.
Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".
About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".
Meanwhile in Germany, Timur told the BBC he was impressed by how lifelike the game was.
"It really feels like a life simulation with the amount of in-game encounters," he said.
The Guardian's Keza MacDonald , external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.
"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.
"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".
From the memes to the music - from the controversies to the culture - you have your say on GTA 6 with Newsbeat's Jordan Kenny and De-Graft Mensah.

After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.
Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".
The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.
On Monday, 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually , external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis , Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."
Democrats won Congress in a blue wave. Now comes the hard part.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art: The Ferrari drivers have previously compromised their own races while battling in Italy and Mexico this season
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc face yet another tense discussion over their ability to race together cleanly on track after colliding in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
Leclerc tipped Hamilton into a spin with 22 laps to go, costing both points in a race where at one stage they were racing with the McLarens, who finished on the podium.
Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, which meant he finished 10th, three places behind Hamilton, in a race won by Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

It was the second race-compromising incident within three grands prix, and it came after the drivers had been brought together to clear the air at the last race in Brazil after their first-lap fighting in Mexico cost them a win.
Hamilton said such an incident "should never happen" but added that: "The question should be for Ferrari now."
Team principal Frederic Vasseur described the situation as "completely unacceptable".
The Frenchman said: "It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsor, the same speech as after Mexico.

"We passed the message to Charles to not overtake because in this kind of race you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you're passed by others. It means you have to do your race and Charles clearly made a mistake.

"It's penalising the team a lot and it's completely unacceptable. Honestly we are more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico, we had a chat together in Brazil, today we passed the message to think about the team when racing together and the outcome is this one."

The battle between the two drivers has been tense all season, and in the second part of the year there have been a series of flashpoints, whether it be on-track racing, disputes about how best to work through strategy, and Hamilton ignoring two separate calls to pit in different races, both of which compromised his result, because he was looking at beating Leclerc.
Hamilton said: "It's not something I want to really get into."
The seven-time champion, who struggled against Leclerc last year but who has been revived in 2026, deflected questions about whether he should be given number-one status.
"I've never asked to be number one," he said. "I genuinely haven't ever asked.
"There was a point in the season where I was 40-odd points ahead, and at that point, the fight was with me and Kimi (Antonelli).
"I was the closest one to him. I was second for a long time in the year.
"At that point, we needed backing to make sure we beat Kimi. There were a few instances in the season where, with the support, I think we could have beaten Kimi.
"But no, that's not what I've asked for. We shouldn't have gotten together. That should just never happen. But I've said everything I can on it, and the question should be for Ferrari now."

Before the incident, the drivers expressed their differing views on team radio, Leclerc expressing his concern for the way Hamilton was defending, Hamilton saying they should be focused on catching the cars in front.
Leclerc said: "He needs to be careful with this squeezing because it's not going to end well."
Hamilton swore as he asked the team to tell Leclerc to "back off", adding: "I'm trying to catch these guys ahead."
This was similar to their different stances in Mexico, when Leclerc was attacking Hamilton on the first lap while the Briton felt they should be working together to defend their one-two positions.
Vasseur said he would talk to the drivers the day after the race, once the immediate heat of the situation had dissipated.
Max Verstappen said George Russell's lock-up was "karma" for his comments about the Dutchman earlier in the Las Vegas weekend
Max Verstappen sealed his fourth win of the season with a stunning victory at a chaotic Las Vegas Grand Prix.
The Red Bull driver fought off his rivals for the lead throughout the race and crossed the line ahead of the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

George Russell, who started second, locked up late on attempting a move on Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli and finished ninth, while Charles Leclerc was given a 10-second time penalty for making contact with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton.
Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Vegas.

A superb display of racecraft. Inherited pole after Kimi Antonelli's grid penalty and spent virtually the entire race being attacked, passed and then finding a way back through, while also working out the optimum energy deployment from inside his Red Bull. One of his finest victories.

A remarkable recovery after dropping as low as 11th in the madness of the opening part of the race. Had genuine pace throughout and fought all the way back to second, finishing less than a second behind Verstappen.

One of the drives of the race. Qualified seventh but started 17th because of his engine penalty and charged all the way through to the podium, gaining 14 places and joining McLaren team-mate Norris in passing Antonelli right at the end.

Fastest of everyone in qualifying and a genuine contender for victory despite starting sixth because of his engine penalty. Battled Verstappen superbly before his Mercedes' energy deployment problem on the final lap cost him two places, although he still recovered fourth from Pierre Gasly before the flag.
An excellent weekend and comfortably Alpine's best result of the season. Reached Q3, stayed with the leading group throughout and was less than three seconds away from victory at the finish.
Another huge result for Alpine. Qualified inside the top 10, stayed out of trouble while plenty around him didn't and converted ninth on the grid into sixth place.

A messy weekend but there was still plenty of fight in the race. Missing Q3 was disappointing and the 10-second time penalty for passing Norris off the circuit was harsh, although being spun by Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc later on was not his fault and he recovered to finish seventh.

A superb recovery from 20th on the grid after his power-unit penalty. Kept himself in contention throughout, made up 12 places and even pinched eighth from Russell at the line to secure Williams' joint-best result of the season.

For 48 laps this was heading towards a very high score. Fastest in both second and final practice, qualified third and spent most of the race going toe-to-toe with Verstappen for the lead. But locking up and putting it into the barrier with two laps remaining was an enormous and costly mistake.

A frustrating weekend from start to finish. Ferrari's qualifying struggles left him 11th and although he recovered well enough to finish sixth on the road, spinning his team-mate Hamilton earned a 10-second time penalty and dropped him to 10th.
A solid weekend without quite finding the points. Led Audi in qualifying and again in the race, eventually finishing 11th after spending much of the evening embroiled in the midfield fight.
Similar story to team-mate Hulkenberg but just a little further back. Started 13th, finished 12th and narrowly held off Haas' Oliver Bearman at the flag.
A very good recovery after starting last because of power-unit penalties. Climbed nine positions, raced aggressively with both Audis and finished only two-tenths behind Bortoleto.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Stepping into a job like Mauricio Pochettino has done at Manchester United , where managers have come and gone frequently, will always lead you to wonder why the others have not lasted very long.
Irrespective of results, you face these first few days in your new post with suspicion.
So, while what happens in Pochettino's first game against Liverpool on Sunday is important, it will not define his early opinions of the club - good or bad.
Whenever you take over a team in mid-season, which I did on a few occasions, you don't usually get much time to work with your players before your first game.

Jumping straight in and going straight to the heart of a two-day preparation for a game, like Pochettino has done before United go to Anfield, is so difficult and I am not sure any manager can honestly make a profound difference.

A change of voice helps, I'm sure, but so does showing strength and confidence in your own principles and making sure the players understand you demand complete and utter commitment in all the games you face, starting with this one.

With time on the training ground being so limited, my initial work would focus on us being a team and working up and down the pitch together, by breaking down different scenarios inside the game and what we should do in them.
I'd keep the focus on hard work and making us difficult to beat - clean sheets are so under-rated.
Then, on the day, your first pre-match speech is always a massive one, and it will be the same for Pochettino too.

My first team talk would always focus on generating an 'us against the world' mentality. As a manager coming in now, you've usually got the job because the team has struggled, so you can play on that to motivate the players.

You can use media reports and stories to show the negativity against them - but then counter that by producing a real 'stand-up and be counted' kind of rallying call, before sending them out on the pitch, while mentioning your faith in them to succeed.
Pochettino had his first training session with United's players on Thursday
I would have selected my team before I met the players, through my own knowledge and also with help from within.

Whichever club I went in at, I'd expect to know something about most of the players within the group in terms of their position and ability, but understanding the character of the squad was vital too.

The existing staff would know more about the lads' qualities in that respect than myself or anyone who had just arrived with me, so I'd always discuss that with the people I had inherited, from fitness coaches to the medical department.

It's what your own eyes tell you that is most important, however. Going into your first game gives you the opportunity to see for yourself what your players are made of - and it can be a completely different view from what other people see.
Most of the early games I managed would be hit and miss in terms of selection, but I would quickly work out the strengths and weaknesses of the group.
As I've mentioned in previous columns, one of my first aims at any club where I was manager was about putting out a team, not a group of individuals.
It does not take long to see when that is not happening. I can remember my first game of my first spell at Stoke, a 4-2 defeat at Walsall in the Championship.

I wasn't universally enamoured by certain crowd favourites in that team and, while any manager knows that leaving some of them out could have an adverse effect on the supporters' view of yourself, you have to stand up and make decisions based on what you see.
It is the same if there are other issues with the squad you have inherited too.
Bruno Fernandes has scored in each of his past two games for Manchester United
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes says he has been offered a new contract by the club but feels it "is not the right time" for discussions about his future.
The 32-year-old midfielder is out of contract at the end of the season , though the club have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until 2028.
He was left out of the side under previous manager Michael Carrick but says he has no issues at the club and has chosen to stay at Old Trafford despite offers elsewhere in recent seasons.
He told Sky Sports: , external "The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay.
"There's no negotiations ongoing, but I've seen people saying that 'he's asked for more money, he's asked for more years'. If I wanted more money, I wouldn't be here.
"I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.
"Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here."
United chief executive Omar Berrada recently spoke about Fernandes' contract situation, saying: "It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private."
Fernandes has scored 75 Premier League goals since signing from Sporting in 2020 and last season set a record for the most assists in a Premier League season.
His form has tailed off this season in a poor start for the club as a whole.
United are 19th in the Premier League table going into Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge against rivals Liverpool on Sunday afternoon.
"We spoke about the contract at the end of last season," Fernandes said.

"We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.
"The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games."
'He will see what Man Utd are made of' - Pulis on Pochettino's first game
Fernandes was dropped for the Premier League defeat by Bournemouth last month after being critical of United's approach in their heavy defeat against Como in the Champions League.
But Fernandes says he did not fall out with Carrick, who was sacked on 12 November.

"The manager came to speak to me before the Bournemouth game, to say: 'Look, I'm not going to start you tomorrow. There's nothing to do with the words of Como, I know people will make it around that. I just want to tell you that we need to change something, I need to make a change, performances have not been great, so I just want you to know that there's nothing to do with that'," Fernandes said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Arsenal are six points behind third-placed London City Lionesses in the Women's Super League
Before the 2026-27 season began, Arsenal technical director Jodie Taylor declared: "I'll flat out say it: we want to win the league and want to take that next step."
After finishing second last season, it seemed like a logical statement to make.
However, after 10 games in this season's Women's Super League, they are sixth in the table, trailing leaders Chelsea by 13 points.
They are also nine points behind third-placed London City Lionesses, albeit with a game in hand, and facing stiff competition to qualify for the Champions League again next campaign.
BBC Sport looks at where things have gone wrong for the Gunners, who have not won the WSL since 2018-19.
Only bottom side Charlton have fewer home points than Arsenal this season
Last term, Arsenal hosted all 11 of their league home games at Emirates Stadium for the first time, winning eight times and drawing on three occasions.
This season, Renee Slegers' side have drawn all five of their home games and will seek their first win at the sixth attempt when they host West Ham on Sunday (14:30 GMT), live on BBC Two.
Two of those draws came against promoted sides Crystal Palace and Birmingham City, where a combined 57 shots yielded just one goal.
Home fans are getting disgruntled and this has been reflected in attendances. Last season, the Gunners had an average attendance of 33,808, better than eight Premier League clubs.
So far this year their biggest crowd was against London City Lionesses last weekend, when 32,588 were in the stands.
Speaking on the Women's Football Weekly podcast, former England striker Ellen White said: "The Emirates seems [like] a bit of an issue for them at the moment - they just can't get that win there.
"A draw might feel like a loss for them because they are so far behind now in terms of the Champions League spots."

Former Gunners striker Vivianne Miedema, who did play at Emirates Stadium for Arsenal but joined Manchester City before the full switch was made, added: "Players always say that the crowd really, really helps you at Arsenal. The fans are amazing - it gives you that extra bit of energy.
"Obviously playing in the Emirates with all the fans should still give them that boost but it doesn't seem to be fully working for them this season so far."
Alessia Russo has scored nine goals in all competitions for Arsenal this season

The Gunners have had 199 shots in 10 league matches but managed just 11 goals. That is just over one goal per game, and their conversion rate of 5.53% is the lowest of any club over the past six seasons.
Part of the problem could be an over-reliance on key goalscorer Alessia Russo.
She has alternated between the number nine and number 10 position during the season but thrives most when she is the focal point in the attack.
This season, the England striker has five league goals and provided two assists, with her form improving in recent weeks.
She was player of the match against Tottenham after scoring and providing an assist in a 2-1 win and similarly against Liverpool, when she scored twice to help Arsenal triumph by the same scoreline.
After Russo, only Lisa Baum (two), Georgia Stanway (two), Smilla Holmberg and Frida Maanum have scored in the league.

Injuries to attacking options Chloe Kelly, Selina Cerci and Stina Blackstenius have also proved costly, while key midfielder Mariona Caldentey is about halfway through an expected 10-week absence with a hamstring injury.
The result is that Arsenal and Brighton are the only teams in the league to have a goal difference of zero after 10 games.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Having lost at home to Argentina in November and then beating Argentina away from home in July, Scotland's next joust with the Pumas is set for Twickenham next Sunday, 29 November - fourth from the northern hemisphere versus fourth from the south on the final day of the Nations Championship.
The warm-up act before the grand final between France and South Africa later on Sunday is not where Scotland wanted to be, but four wins from six games is a decent return.
A fifth win in seven would be encouraging, if not life-changing for this team. They've all been at this rodeo before.
On Saturday, Scotland's much-changed team tore an understrength, over-powered and severely out-matched Japan to shreds. Eleven tries was bordering on an exhibition.

It didn't tell us anything we didn't already know about head coach Gregor Townsend's set-up, but it was a special day for a number of people, chief among them the fantastically promising Liam McConnell and the revitalised Darcy Graham - hat-tricks for both and a ton of other wonderful moments besides.
Scotland kept 'foot on throat' in ruthless display - captain McDowall
That Scotland had far too much speed, skill, power and ruthlessness for Japan was not surprising. They scored some blistering tries.

These are fine rugby players, albeit ones who are, just like the players they took over from, prone to giving up soft moments; avoidable penalties, easy entries into their own 22, self-inflicted stress on their own defence, which was strong on Saturday.

Scotland gave up seven penalties in the first half against Japan. The visitors weren't good enough to break their hosts down from all that field position, but the teams that Scotland want to start beating certainly would have been.
New Zealand were more than good enough only a few weeks ago. It was a large part of Scotland's fall that day.
In public, Townsend accentuates the positives, as he must - and there was plenty of positivity to go around. His team delivered a thunderous and classy win.
Privately, he has to be looking at the indiscipline of the first half - it was near- perfect in the second - and cursing it.

Japan were never going to punish them, but in defining games in the Six Nations against heavy hitters, and in the knockouts of the World Cup against bigger beasts, then he knows what's going to happen if that stuff gets repeated.
This is unforgiving terrain. Scotland are desperate to move closer to a higher level and so they will be brutal on each other - or should be.

We saw what that level was all about on Saturday - a fast-improving England brutalising the All Blacks, who have now lost back-to-back, and a ferociously physical Ireland taking down the Springboks, who have also now lost two-in-a-row.

The standard is savagely high. Critics of Townsend say that Scotland haven't improved on his watch because they haven't won any trophies. That pays no regard to the improvement that other nations have made in the Townsend years.
It's not like the biggest countries are standing still. South Africa aren't, France aren't.
Ireland looked for a while like they were falling away a touch but now they appear to be back. England are flying.

New Zealand are a work-in-progress, but they were too much for Scotland. Scotland are moving forward, but for all the tries and all the thrills they can produce, they have a long way to go, if they get there at all. They know that better than anybody.
Edinburgh flanker Liam McConnell was the darling of fans at a packed Murrayfield

Murrayfield was heaving again on Saturday, a capacity crowd for the visit of Japan, 12,000 more fans for this game against the world number 12 than turned up at the Principality Stadium last weekend for Wales playing the All Blacks.
Wales head coach Steve Tandy said he was frustrated as his side failed to back up their epic win over New Zealand, narrowly losing to Australia.
The Wallabies edged the Nations Championship Test 29-26 in Cardiff on Saturday, a week after a first Wales victory over the All Blacks since 1953 had led to wild celebrations.
Taniela Tupou, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau secured a try-bonus point for Australia as Ryan Lonergan and Carter Gordon added nine points with the boot.
Wales also scored four tries, through Dewi Lake's double, Blair Murray and Ryan Elias, with Sam Costelow landing three conversions.
"The overarching feeling is the frustration of losing," said Tandy.
"We were disappointed. We probably weren't as accurate as we could have been. We were held up three times and could have gone ahead on the scoreboard."
The 46-year-old former Ospreys coach added: "Maybe we needed a little bit of composure but there were enough opportunities to come away with the win.
"I know it's not the result anyone wanted but the supporters were amazing again."
Despite the loss, and that frustration, the Wales head coach praised his side's attitude in attempting to follow up their historic win against the All Blacks.
"Fair play to the boys, after such a monumental game last week with the emotional energy, we stuck in the game and scored four tries," he said.
"So there are a lot of positives in the performance to take as well."
Nations Championship - Australia triumph over Wales - reaction
Dewi Lake has scored three tries in the past two internationals

Australia, having soaked up fierce first-half pressure, produced some fine attacking rugby after the break to prevent Wales from winning three matches in a row for the first time since the 2023 World Cup.

Fiji claimed their first win in the Nations Championship following their 21-16 win over Italy in Udine on Sunday morning.
The result meant all three Pacific Island teams Fiji, Samoa and Tonga recorded wins at the weekend in their respective World Rugby internationals.
Tonga had thrashed Hong Kong China 55-19 in Hong Kong on Saturday night in their Nations Cup clash, while Samoa walloped Spain 90-22 earlier today.
In Udine, the story truly belonged to Fiji and their second half resurgence as the islanders romp to the victory, silencing the Italian crowd that had cheered their side on.
The result means the two teams will go head to head again in London in the weekend, with the two both finishing sixth in their respective South and Northern hemisphere pools.
Fiji scored three tries to Italy's one, with captain Tevita Ikanivere claiming two, while flanker and 'Player of the Match' Kitione Salawa adding another.
Flyhalves Ben Volavola and his replacement Caleb Muntz added the extra six points between them.
Italy scored their only try through captain Lorenzo Cannone, with fullback Tommaso Allan adding 11 points through a conversion and three penalties.
Man of the match performer Salawa said post-match the Italians were tough and thanked his fellow players for staying in the fight until the end.
"First of all I would like to than the Lord Almighty for giving us the strength today," he said.
"I would also like to thank the boys for the great effort against the Italian boys.
"Thank the Italian boys for giving us a hard battle tonight and our boys for staying in the fight."
Italy were fierce on defence and lightning on attack, keeping smiles on their fans' faces in the first half.
Fiji's Nathan Hughes was the first to receive the ball as Italy kicked off and the two teams tested each other out in the first seven minutes.
The Italians drew first blood in the game after captain Lorenzo Cannone crashed over the Fijians' line and planted the ball across, despite Hughes' attempted tackle.
That came in the eighth minute, following a good break from halfback Stephen Varney, that sliced open the Fijian midfield, and fullback Tommaso Allan's conversion gave them an early 7-0 lead.
Fijian captain Tevita Ikanivere was penalised for playing ball on ground in the 12th minute and Allan extended the home team's lead to 10-0 from inside Fiji's 22 metre zone.
But Fiji came back hard and a lineout take inside the Italian's 22 metres saw Ikanivere dive over for their try. Flyhalf Ben Volavola converted, as Italy led 10-7.
Italy's defensive efforts after the 20th minute saw them stop three scoring opportunities from their visitors, managing three good turnovers as Fiji attacked.
A second Allan penalty in the 31st minute saw Fiji trailed their host 13-7 at halftime.
Fiji's Tevita Ikanivere leads an attack against Italy. Photo: Fiji Rugby Union
Fiji started the second half with a lot more determination, with prop Peni Ravai running on to a lineout win and driving his way through the Italian defence.

That saw Italy defending desperately on their line but they could not stop Ikanivere from diving over in between the posts in the 44th minute, with replacement flyhalf Caleb Muntz tipping the conversion over as Fiji claimed the lead 14-13.
That spurred Fiji into action with two consecutive bombs from Frank Lomani forcing errors in the Italian defence.
Taranaki Bulls reps Marika Parker in for his debut for Fiji, having played for Taranaki Bulls National Provincial Championship.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2731675: And perhaps the worst thing about it was the way one of sport's most remarkable identities has been publicly eviscerated, William Wallace style, in consecutive weeks.
By which I mean the character of invincibility. Once, so imposing, so persuasive, so effective for the All Blacks. Once, almost self-fulfilling.
Remember Dublin, in 2013? The All Blacks were trailing 17 - 22 going into injury time. But Richie McCaw knew that team wouldn't lose. And the team believed him. And they were right.
At that stage, the Irish had never beaten the All Blacks. Not once. In 111 years. And it wasn't going to happen under Richie's watch.

Wales? They so deserved their victory two Saturdays ago (their time). But that was a team that had almost forgotten what the V was for. Losing had become a habit. Then they beautifully upended New Zealand. Whoopsie-daisy.

The terrible thing, as I watched the game against England in a kind of solitary penitence for all the victories I wasn't grateful enough for, is that I began to look at my phone. Then I turned the commentary down and listened to new music. Really. At 4am.

Not long ago, there was a certain inevitability about the narrative arc. The Northern Hemisphere teams would play like stink for sixty or seventy minutes, casting themselves as Robin Hood, and then the All Blacks would grind mercilessly past them, and the foregone conclusion would be manifest.

I mean, it wasn't always that simple. I'm being reductive. But the facts tell their own story. 111 years for Ireland. A 73-year gap for Wales. England now really, really having the measure of us (Ouch.) All of that happening in very recent years.
There's nothing aberrant about this. It's not unusual, to cruelly use that famous Welsh songline. What were exceptional were the winning streaks, not their end.
But, gosh, we look flat-footed in our response. And skittish, too, if you can be both at the same time.

New Zealand players after the 3rd England try. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport
Take the coaches. As opposed to taking to the coaches, which NZ Rugby likes to do.

Remember August 2022? NZ Rugby's CEO, Mark Robinson, actually flew to South Africa, during the tour, to knock on Ian Foster's hotel room door, death-row warden like, before the players mounted a passionate defence of their coach by winning at Ellis Park.
And then, it was Scott Robertson. Billed as the new messiah. Ridiculously oversold, the poor man. Who could possibly live up to that billing? Not him, as it turned out.

New Zealand Rugby conducted a review (the phrase, "physician, heal thyself" springs to mind here), which is seldom good news when the review is of you. Sure enough, it was agreed he should go. (Agreed. Lol.) It felt shabby from the top. Great teams aren't led like that. (And the players see it and know that bell tolls for them, too.)

Leicester Fainga'anuku as a back and a forward? Really? Why don't we just make him the best one-of-the above that that gorgeously gifted (but not superhuman) player can possibly be? Richie Mo'unga recalled to the All Blacks after a three-year absence. Ruben Love was injured, yes. But it still felt hopeful, a coin toss, rather than a meaningful investment in something long-term.

Fehi Fineanganofo, so brilliant with the Hurricanes that NZ Rugby lassoed him to hold him back from a lucrative deal with Newcastle. He got injured, sure. But if he was good enough to retain, he's good enough to play.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2730280: The All Blacks, humbled at Twickenham by England in another historic defeat, will look for answers over the next couple of days as they prepare to face the same foe at the same venue in a bid for third place in the Nations Championship.

Needing a win to keep the pressure on South Africa for top spot on their side of the draw to qualify for next weekend's top playoff place, New Zealand instead put in their worst performance of the year in losing 37-12 to the rampant English .

It was a step down even from their loss to Wales in Cardiff last weekend, their first defeat to the Welsh since 1953, and will put pressure on head coach Dave Rennie and his assistants Neil Barnes, Mike Blair, Tana Umaga and Jason Ryan.

Such was their lethargy over the 80 minutes - despite what should have been the hugely motivating factors of their Nations Championship position and milestones celebrated by Beauden Barrett (150 tests) and Anton Lienert-Brown (100) - they were utterly dominated and there now is a very real chance they will lose for the third week in succession.
It means they are on the brink of their worst season of the professional era. Another defeat would take Rennie's record in his first year to seven wins and six losses - the worst since 1949.

The All Blacks' shocking defeat in south west London - their worst ever to England - meant South Africa needed only a losing bonus point from their test against Ireland in Dublin a couple of hours later to take top spot and the world champions delivered in a 20-17 defeat .
Head coach Dave Rennie and skipper Codie Taylor face the media after the All Blacks' loss.
The 'Boks will play France in a mouth-watering clash for the inaugural title which will come a fortnight after the French held off the world champions in a thriller in Paris.
The main themes from Rennie's press conference were his disappointment at the performance and result and a desire to get to the bottom of why his men did not deliver.

Asked whether he had full faith in his players and his assistant coaches, Rennie replied: "I've got no doubt about the quality of the people that we have. It was a poor night but from a playing perspective we have excellent men [and] staffing wise we have a great group."
And yet, after conceding five tries to Wales in Cardiff the All Blacks again conceded five to England.
They were far too easily breached - as they have been many times this year - and the focus will go on defence coach Umaga.

Forwards coaches Neil Barnes and Jason Ryan will not escape scrutiny either - the All Blacks' set piece was again second best (they lost four lineouts on their own throw including two in a row in the second half) and the pack lacked bite and aggression at the breakdown in spite of the promise to respond appropriately to last weekend's disappointment.

Blair, the backs coach, may have questions to answer about an attack that was far too lateral and produced only one piece of true continuity - a superb try for Beauden Barrett in which the 35-year-old fullback sprinted in untouched from 40m out.

"It's disappointing," Rennie said. "We'll spend the next couple of days trying to work out why. We felt the preparation was good. It was a motivating factor to perform well tonight. We were well short.

"There was no lack of effort or heart. With a team like England you've got to try to apply some pressure and most of our footy we played in our end of the field. At halftime we had made 130 tackles to their 39 so maybe that told in the end.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2727564: The Breakers remain on the bottom of the Australian basketball league ladder, after an agonising 94-91 defeat to Melbourne United.

Mennenga ended the half with 14 points and five rebounds, while Davison worked his way to seven points and three assists as the Breakers went to halftime down 50-44.
The third quarter went tit-for-tat, as the Breakers twice closed to within a basket, but Melbourne kept their composure, to eventually extend their lead to eight, 74-66 with one quarter to play.
In the fourth, Melbourne led once again by as much as 11 points, before the Breakers stormed back of some stellar scoring from Mojave King.
They tied the game inside the final minute, but Davison missing a shot with 14 seconds to play proved costly, and paved the way for Melbourne to hang on for a three point win.

New recruit Skylar Mays top scored for the Breakers with a game high 27 points, five rebounds and five assists, while Davison finished with 11 points and 10 assists, Mennenga 16 points and nine rebounds, and King, 15 points.
The defeat is the Breakers 11th from 16 games this season, but they've lost six of those matches be fewer than six points.
They now need a big pre-Christmas period, to stay in touch for the playoffs, as they are now two wins outside the top six.
Their next game is a rematch against Melbourne on 4 December, following a FIBA international window.

But most focused on how strong England had been, making them potentially impossible to beat.

The Guardian's analysis piece started off by reminding everyone that last week's loss to Wales was met with heavy criticism that the All Blacks had let down their country, even from coach Dave Rennie.
"What awaits the All Blacks after this? Public humiliation? Exile? A firing squad at dawn?"

New Zealand players after the 3rd England try. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport
But the article doesn't encourage a punishment, in fact it criticises Rennie for his own harshness.

"Perhaps it is wise to remember it is only a game, Dave. For what made the very best All Blacks sides so impressive was that they always looked like they were having fun ... This rabble did not look like they were having much fun out there."
Planet Rugby gave it's five key takeaways from the game with the first focusing on the "statement" England made.
"England made a statement with a convincing and, at times, exhilarating 37-12 win."

"We are witnessing something very, very special here, an identity being crafted. This England side played with a swagger and a confidence we haven't seen in a white shirt for some time, and it was joyous rugby."
The article also pointed out the game proved "shirt numbers don't matter".

Josh Moorby of New Zealand is tackled. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport
"At times you'd have wondered whether the two sides had put on the wrong colour shirts, and nowhere was that clearer than in the way England's forwards ignored the numbers on their backs.
"Ollie Chessum wore 6, but in defence he dropped into the second row and Alex Coles took the blindside edge and then they swapped back when England had the ball."
"England fired a warning to their rivals ahead of next year's World Cup."
The article started strong in contemplating what this win might mean for the future of both teams.
It also credited some of England's victorious morale to the presence of former captain Lewis Moody, who was diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease in October 2025.
"The presence of Moody... visibly lifted Maro Itoje's men to set the scene for a five-try rout that registered back-to-back wins against New Zealand for the first time since 2002 and 2003."
The All Blacks' morale on the other hand was cited as lacking an energy many expected after their previous loss.
"The backlash expected after New Zealand's shock defeat to Wales last Saturday never materialised, instead they played like a tired team with the weight of the world on their shoulders."

The City Kickboxing product landed a vicious right hook at the end of the second round, forcing referee Marc Goddard to step in for the stoppage victory.
Stirling did exactly what he said he would, taking his time before launching an assault at the wild Czech fighter.
The opening exchanges saw both tentative to throw anything too risky, with Stirling finding a home for his low kicks, and Procházka's jab peppering his opponent from afar.
For a moment in the first round it looked as if Stirling had been dropped by an overhand right, but replays showed it was a slip as the two light heavyweights closed in on each other.

Currently champion and teammate Carlos Ulberg won the belt after knocking out Procházka in April.
Stirling has previously said he would wait his turn for the title, and the pair wouldn't need to fight for the belt.
Asked who he wanted next in his post-fight speech, Stirling said anyone ranked above him, and instead, made a bigger case for custom shorts.

England have scored five tries in thrashing the All Blacks 37-12 at Twickenham , the visitors losing their fifth test of the year and compounding last weekend's historic defeat to Wales with a lethargic and disconnected effort.
Their set piece was poor and their discipline again not up to the required standard.
Defensively it was easily their worst performance since they were embarrassed by South Africa in Wellington last year and, in scoring only two tries, their attack was error-ridden and toothless.
The 25-point margin of defeat was the All Blacks' largest against England.

The All Blacks promised to respond to last weekend's defeat in Cardiff . They failed to do so by making history for the wrong reasons - again - and there will be questions now about the quality of the advice the players are receiving from their coaches and indeed the ability of those players to plot their way out of trouble on the field.

The All Blacks' Nations Championship position is probably the last thing head coach Dave Rennie was thinking about at the final whistle but the No.1 Southern Hemisphere seeding and place in the top playoff is now South Africa's to lose when they play Ireland in Dublin.
Rennie and company will now undergo a huge amount of pressure to salvage something from the wreckage of the past couple of weekends.
Next weekend's playoff against an opponent yet to be decided will provide this team with another huge challenge and the potential for yet another defeat.
The All Blacks last lost five tests in a year in 1998. They lost six matches in 1949.

Captain Codie Taylor said afterwards: "We were just really inaccurate tonight… we put ourselves under pressure… when we had our opportunities we gave the ball away or made errors. Pretty disappointing."
The All Blacks hardly touched the ball in the first quarter of a test that, overall, lacked real drama due to England's utter dominance.
Henry Slade was over after five minutes thanks to a neat grubber from No.10 Fin Smith and the All Blacks response was to lose an attacking lineout. They lost four in total on their own throw.
England, emboldened by the All Blacks' failures and their success in consistently winning the gain line, kept the pressure on.

After being held up over the line they were in again via halfback Jack van Portvliet, although his success in crossing the line by diving over an attacking ruck was debatable in terms of its legality.
Worse was to come. Outstanding No.8 Ben Earl, a well deserved man of the match, scored an individual try from an attacking scrum - a defensive failure that will hurt badly.

With time ticking down to halftime and the All Blacks staring at a 19-0 deficit, they needed something to cling on to and it came in the form of a solid attacking lineout drive and a try from prop Ethan de Groot.
It was only the second time in the half that the All Blacks had been inside the England 22.

Rennie's men began the second half presumably knowing that their defence needed immediate improvement - they conceded five line breaks to zero in the first stanza, with regular centre Quinn Tupaea badly missed, as most expected.
Their contestable kicks were too deep, leaving the men in black watched as England counter-attacked and breached almost immediately.
Two lineout losses followed - England maintaining their shape - and, roared on by a crowd of 82,000, Ollie Chessum burst through Will Jordan's tackle to score in the corner for England's fourth try.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm8e: The audio appeared to be coming from behind the judges during Saturday's episode (file photo)
The BBC has apologised "for any offence caused" after lewd audio was heard during the live broadcast of Strictly Come Dancing.

A recording of sex noises appeared to be playing from the audience in Blackpool's Tower Ballroom as judge Motsi Mabuse gave feedback early in Saturday's episode. She paused before joking: "It's not me."

At the end of the programme, presenter Emma Willis apologised to viewers "if you heard any audio disruptions". A BBC spokesperson also issued an apology and said it was "investigating how this happened".
Lancashire police said it was assessing whether any criminal offences may have taken place, after receiving a formal complaint and a mobile phone being seized.

The moment was streamed on social media by content creator Daniel Jarvis, whose videos include pranks. He appeared to place a phone call before the audio began playing in the ballroom, and suggested he was trying to target judge Craig Revel Horwood for his "bullying".
Jarvis has previously claimed he was responsible for sex noises disrupting Match of the Day in 2023 .
Willis told viewers: "Before we see the judges' leaderboard, we'd like to apologise if you heard any audio disruptions earlier in tonight's show and for any offence caused."
A BBC spokesperson said in a statement: "We apologise to any viewers offended during the live broadcast of Strictly this evening.
An edit will be made to the programme available on BBC iPlayer.
A spokesperson for Lancashire Constabulary said: "We are aware of an incident that took place during the filming of Strictly Come Dancing in Blackpool.
"We have been in contact with the event organisers, and a formal complaint has been made to us.
"A mobile phone has been seized and we are now looking into the matter to see if any criminal offences have taken place."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4g: I Am Helen charts a relationship spiralling after a non-consensual sexual experience
If you want to unwind on the sofa after a long day, I Am Helen probably isn't the show for you.
The Channel 4 drama starring Bridgerton star Nicola Coughlan and Joe Cole from Peaky Blinders has been called a must-watch by critics - but the cast don't want viewers sitting comfortably.
"There's going to be a few awkward sofas," Cole, who plays Helen's partner Steve, says.
"There's going to be people up and down the country that will be able to relate to this in varying degrees.
"And if we can put that in their living rooms and open up a debate, open up a conversation - and maybe help people be better - then we've done our job."
I Am Helen is the latest project in director Dominic Savage's I Am... series, female-led stories focusing on themes like mental health and relationships.
The two fully-improvised episodes, devised in collaboration with Coughlan, follow a relationship spiralling after Steve tries to choke Helen during sex without consent.
"We never realised how incredibly timely it would be," Coughlan tells BBC Newsbeat.
"It feels incredibly relevant right now, and specifically right now, because pornography that includes strangulation has just been outlawed in the UK."
Earlier this month, the government made it illegal for anyone to possess or publish porn that shows strangulation or suffocation.
That decision followed a review last year that found choking was "rife" on porn sites and had become normalised, particularly among younger people.
Coughlan and Cole say they were keen to make everything about their characters and the setting as relatable as possible to emphasise the shocking fallout.

"We needed one inciting incident that felt like something that could really plausibly happen between a couple, that it just goes slightly too far without consent, and it just blows everything up," Coughlan says.
"It's really important we see Steve's perspective in it because it makes him a normal guy.
"He's not this evil guy who's attacking Helen. He does bad things, but he's complicated. And hopefully you see them both as real people."
Bridgerton star Nicola Coughlan collaborated with director Dominic Savage on the drama
Filming the series without a script meant the actors were fully immersed in their characters, making them real not just for viewers but for themselves too.
"I'm not playing myself, but there's far less, let's say 'character' here than anything else I've ever done because a lot of this is about just reacting," Coughlan says.
She and Cole would film long takes, some lasting about an hour and often with heated exchanges, which might need to be shot multiple times.
Coughlan describes I Am Helen as "the most challenging thing in terms of material that I've ever worked on", adding for the first time in a role she needed counselling.
"You literally would be physically and mentally quite exhausted," she says.

"There were times that I said to Dominic [Savage] if he wanted to do a third take for example - and I've never said this before on set - but I actually don't think I have that in me because you hit a wall.
"When you're given that freedom, things happen and I think you can get some really interesting and also quite shocking stuff," he says.
For him, that came when he damaged a fridge on set with a punch.
But it's that authenticity of emotion which, while difficult for the actors, is what Coughlan thinks makes the series so engaging.
"When people watch the 'I Ams', they feel quite truthful," she says.
Joe Cole and Nicola Coughlan wanted the fallout to feel plausible in a normal relationship

A Brent councillor has joined calls to prevent Marilyn Manson performing at Wembley Stadium next year ahead of a trial the singer faces over sexual assault allegations.
Liberal Democrat Anton Georgiou has gathered more than 20,000 signatures on a petition urging the venue to take "a firm stand" against Manson, who is due to support Slipknot there in July.
Manson, whose real name is Brian Warner, is due to stand trial next November in a civil lawsuit brought by his former assistant Ashley Walters, who alleges sexual abuse. He denies the allegation.
Georgiou has written to the promoter Live Nation and Wembley Stadium urging the organisers to cancel the performance until a verdict is reached.

Manson has faced multiple allegations of sexual misconduct from several women, some of which have been dropped or dismissed. He denies all the allegations.

"That does not diminish our commitment to tackling violence against women and girls, which has no place in Brent," they added.

British television, theatre and film star Helen Fraser, who was perhaps best known for her role in the hit prison drama Bad Girls, has died.
The actress, who also appeared in episodes of Coronation Street and The Royle Family, reportedly died on 10 November at Yaxley House Care Home, in Eye, Suffolk. She was 84.
Born in Oldham, Greater Manchester, she had lived in Wickham Skeith, in Suffolk, with her late husband Peter Handford.

From 2004 until 2019, she was also an ambassador for East Anglia's Children's Hospices (EACH). The charity said it was "deeply saddened" by her death and would "remember her with enormous fondness and gratitude".
"Helen was very special to us and a wonderful ambassador, supporter and friend who worked tirelessly to champion our cause," a spokesperson said.
"Whether fundraising, attending events, opening our shops or rallying our volunteers, Helen brought incredible warmth, empathy and joy.
"She had a wonderful way with people and made a lasting impression on all those fortunate enough to spend time in her company."
The actress first trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before making her breakthrough in the 1963 film Billy Liar.
But it was her role as the tough prison officer Sylvia Hollamby in the long-running ITV show Bad Girls that made her a household name among British audiences.
Fraser appeared in more than 90 episodes across all eight series, from 1999 to 2006, and later reprised the role in the West End stage version of Bad Girls: The Musical.
Fraser's funeral will be held at West Suffolk Crematorium on 4 December at 13:30 GMT, according to a death notice published by the East Anglian Daily Times , external .
Attendees are asked to make donations in her honour to East Anglia's Children's Hospices charity.
"We feel truly honoured that EACH will benefit from donations made in her memory at her funeral," the charity's spokesperson added.
