https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq78: Harry Styles has carved out a solo career after One Direction
When Harry Styles was just 16, his mother Anne secretly signed up him up for the ITV's The X Factor talent show in the hope of turning his singing dreams into a reality.
Fast forward more than 15 years later and the 32-year-old is set for a prestigious headline slot at Glastonbury 2027.
Styles will perform on the Pyramid Stage alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish with Cher among the other stars on the bill.
But how exactly did Styles' career rocket from his early years growing up in the Cheshire village of Holmes Chapel to leading one of the most coveted festival sets in the music industry?
Styles attended Hermitage Primary School in his village, which lies just 25 miles (40km) south of Manchester.
His year two teacher Helen Bailey fondly remembers how the seven-year-old "always had a cheeky little smile on his face".
"I just remember him always being really happy, really smiley, really popular with his friends," said Helen, who has worked at the school for 26 years.
Her colleague Kathryn Davies, who taught Styles in year three, also remembers his "cheeky personality".
"He was a real pleasure to teach, you know, across all areas of the curriculum," she said.
"He did have a sense of humour, but he knew when to stop. He had perfect timing, so he never pushed it too far."
One of Styles' performances was filmed for a Netflix show One Night In Manchester
The signs were there from an early age with Styles taking on a number of roles in the school's shows, including the lead role of Barney the mouse in a nativity and a conductor in Bugsy Malone.
"He had what we thought at the time was quite a small part," said Kathryn.
"He was the conductor of the orchestra, but he just knew how to hold the audience.
"He just used to turn around and give a little wink without any training at all.
"This role of conductor - that we thought was quite a small part because he'd have his bigger part in year six - became a bigger part than we anticipated."
Both Helen and Kathryn said they went on to watch with pride as his career blossomed.
"We're proud obviously of all the children, but I think we did see a star in the making when he was at school," said Helen.
For Kathryn, she hopes his career acts as an inspiration to the future generations who attend the school.
"It's nice to see that somebody who starts off here and can become so successful," she said.
"Hopefully the children who are here will see that for themselves and think 'well anybody can live out their dream'."
Styles worked at a bakery in the village of Holmes Chapel while at school
Earlier this year he gave out tickets to his sold-out Manchester show at the Co-op Live Arena to 50 pupils.
"As Harry's ex head teacher I am so pleased that he has kept a place in his heart for his roots and for the village and school where he grew and thrived," said Nigel Bielby at the time.
The village has since become no stranger to so-called "Harries" - as his fans are often dubbed - who travel to Cheshire to explore the place where their idol grew up.
Among the popular destinations is W. Mandeville's bakery, where Styles worked part-time while at school.
There is also a mural that depicts Styles and Cheshire's Twemlow Viaduct, where he reportedly had his first kiss.
This design, by local artists Victoria Holland and Eamonn Murphy, is a riff on popular vintage railway posters

In 2010, Styles travelled to his X Factor audition for his big break, earning a space in what would become the global phenomenon One Direction alongside Niall Horan, Liam Payne, Louis Tomlinson and Zayn Malik.
The boy band went on to release five albums in five years, dominating the music charts worldwide with their pop anthems.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3v: Peter Fluck alongside a satirical puppet of Margaret Thatcher that he created, pictured in 1992
Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.
His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.

Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.
"The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said.
"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added.
"Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."
The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million.
Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art.
Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge.
"You could say we took the traditional newspaper editorial cartoon and put it on the screen," Fluck told ArtCornwall in an interview , external in 2006.
He described the show as being shown "at the difficult time of 10 o'clock on a Sunday night when all politicians should have been in bed".

Many of the characters included parodies of Thatcher's cabinet, with Douglas Hurd depicted with "Mr Whippy ice cream" hair, and her successor John Major caricatured as a dull, grey puppet with a penchant for peas.

"We did get quite a lot of approaches from politicians for their puppet to be made, because if you didn't appear as a puppet on Spitting Image you hadn't made it as a politician," Fluck said in an interview in 2011. , external
It was eventually axed by ITV because of declining audience numbers.

In a statement, the broadcaster said Fluck's "creative contribution to TV satire is simply unrivalled... his cutting edge puppetry and caricature skills, alongside the show's sharp and always shrewdly observed humour, became a defining part of the cultural zeitgeist.
"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his family and friends at this very sad time."
When he stepped away from the show, Fluck moved to Cornwall and focused his art on ceramics, printmaking and mobiles.
In 2018, Law donated his entire archive of Spitting Images to Cambridge University.
The collection - including original scripts, puppet moulds, drawings and recordings - was conserved and held in the library.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4g: Zendaya, Jodie Comer and Sydney Sweeney have all been touted as the next ‘Bond girl’
After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinson’s leading lady?
What’s clear is that Pattinson’s announcement as 007 has completely upped the game.
He's one of Hollywood's biggest stars, so all eyes are on Amazon MGM to see whether they go for an equally big name as a ‘Bond girl’, or if they'll take a chance on someone a little less well known.
Whoever is cast opposite him, though, needs to have a "very strong identity of her own", believes film critic Larushka Ivan-Zadeh - "someone distinctive, sexy, complicated".
Showbiz reporter Catrina Rose agrees: "I'd love to see a Bond girl who's just as interesting and unpredictable as he is."
And then, some say the whole concept of a Bond girl is outdated and the role needs to evolve for a new era. So what can we expect?
No actress has yet confirmed they're in the running - but stars who have been bandied about the internet include Zendaya , whose name shot to the top of the list after Pattinson's casting.
The duo have already shared three films together this year and make a "really exciting pairing," says Ivan-Zadeh.
Rose agrees that as one of the most recognisable actresses in Hollywood, Zendaya is "definitely someone I'd be thinking about now".
But her Euphoria co-stars Hunter Schafer and Sydney Sweeney could give her a run for her money.

There have been rumours about Sweeney getting the role for months, and you can see why, says Dr Llewella Chapman, a film historian at the University of East Anglia. "She has sex appeal and an ability to take on tougher roles too," she tells the BBC.
Sweeney was given a boost last month by former Bond girl Trina Parks, who told the Telegraph she would fit the role well because Bond needed a woman with "ownership over her sexuality".
Robert Pattinson said to be "entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime"
Speculation is also growing over Pattinson’s partner, actor and singer Suki Waterhouse . She once said she’d love to play , external " a bad-ass Bond girl , external ".
But there isn’t a precedent for husband-wife couples in the films, and it may be more likely that she picks up a cameo role, if indeed she wants to.

Meanwhile, TV presenter Maya Jama has picked up new interest following her storming run on Celebrity Traitors. After she quit Love Island , rumours swirled that she could be the next Bond girl - but she’s just signed a Netflix deal, so it’s unclear whether that would still be a possibility.

Another strong contender is Florence Pugh who, like Zendaya, also stars alongside Pattinson in Dune: Part Three. Earlier this week she threw her hat in the ring to be in the new Bond film - although as a villain, rather than his leading lady.

"She ticks quite a few boxes if they're looking for someone bankable," says Rose. "I could absolutely see her as a Bond woman who turns out to be the villain, someone Bond thinks is on his side, but she's actually been playing him the whole time."
Florence Pugh stars alongside Robert Pattinson in Dune: Part Three, reprising her role as Princess Irulan
Queen's Gambit star Anya Taylor-Joy is another name Amazon MGM could be thinking about if they want a big, recognisable actress, as well as Killing Eve's Jodie Comer (Villanelle meets Bond, anyone?)
Meanwhile, Crazy Rich Asians star Gemma Chan told Variety she was "flattered" by fans speculating she could be a Bond girl. "Absolutely I would," she said , external .
Other names that have been floated include Saoirse Ronan, Margaret Qualley, Marisa Abela, Emily Blunt, Lily James, Chase Infiniti, Inde Navarrette, Simone Ashley, Deva Cassel and Ambika Mod .
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jr: A portrait of Daphne du Maurier sent to Fernande, her French finishing school tutor in August 1930
A set of photos of globally renowned 20th century author Daphne du Maurier has been shared by her family for the first time.
The photos show du Maurier in a series of family images, in settings including around Cornwall where she lived and did most of her writing - she died in 1989.
Her eldest grandson Paul de Zulueta found the pictures while researching a new book telling the personal story of his grandmother's artistic dynasty.
He said: "They were all tucked away in my mother's box. She said you might find this amusing - there's a box of photos here."
Du Maurier's novels which include Rebecca, Frenchman's Creek and Jamaica Inn continue to enthral readers, and often make the dark and brooding Cornish landscape central to the story.
Rebecca, written in 1938, has sold about 30 million copies worldwide and several of her novels have been made into TV shows and films.
Her grandson says writing about his ancestors and his famous grandmother has helped him understand her better.
One of the photos shows Paul's grandparents Daphne and Tommy outside Ferryside, around the time of their honeymoon in 1932
De Zulueta was given access to du Maurier's private letters and photos, kept by his mother and his aunt.
His book Last Night I Dreamt tells of her connection to Ferryside, on the banks of the river Fowey in Cornwall, which has been a du Maurier family home for 100 years.
She first stayed there when she was 19, and it is where she wrote her first novel, The Loving Spirit.
Bodinnick, near Fowey, is also where she met her husband, Lt Gen Sir Frederick Browning, affectionately known as Tommy within the family.
When asked to pick two of the photos, De Zulueta referred to one showing the couple walking arm in arm not long after they married, and another of them in a boat.
"This is a particularly nice photograph of Daphne and Tommy in Fowey. Tommy my grandfather was wearing his brown leather jerkin.
"And of course this one is taken just outside of Ferryside in 1932. It must have been around the time of their honeymoon more or less, as they got married in July1932.
Paul De Zulueta recently returned to Fowey to talk about the du Maurier family history at the town's literary festival
De Zueleta visited his grandmother in Fowey as a child every school holiday.
He remembers her being great fun, very mischievous and "someone with a great sense of humour, who filled a room with laughter", rather than the reclusive figure she is often described as.
"And she said when she first came down to Cornwall 'this is the freedom that I have long sought.
"The freedom to write and the freedom to walk, the freedom to be by myself'."
She later moved to Menabilly, the house that was the inspiration for Manderley, the country estate in Rebecca.
Daphne and Tommy out together in Cornwall in early autumn 1933
Daphne (right), Tod (left, the family's housekeeper and governess) and the author's two children Flavia and Kits (standing) basking in the sun outside the east wing of Menabilly in 1952

Rediscovering his grandparents' relationship from the perspective of an adult has been a voyage of discovery for De Zulueta, who now believes his grandfather had Post Traumatic Stress Disorder after the war, for the rest of his life.

Browning's wartime service culminated in commanding airborne forces in the flawed Operation Market Garden, where thousands of troops parachuted into the Netherlands trying to seize key bridges from the Germans.
De Zulueta now recognises the stress his grandfather's absence would have had on the couple and the pressures of war meant "we need to judge the era softly".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crje: In two years, Westside Cowboy have rocketed from the sweaty corners of Manchester's student pub circuit to performances on one of America's biggest talk shows and at many of the UK's biggest festivals.
What started as jamming for fun in a student bedroom has become the latest revolution in British indie known as "Britainicana".
Now the quartet have been named the BBC Introducing Artist of the Year for 2026.
Westside Cowboy join a prestigious list that includes Myles Smith, Olivia Dean, Tom Grennan and several other now household names that have won the award.
It is 3 December 2024 and I am finally about to see Westside Cowboy.
A typical cold winter night on Oldham Street, Manchester, where four students are set to play their first headline show together in the innocuous backroom of a little pub called The Castle Hotel.
Wolstenholme, pictured with Murphy and Bradbury, has championed the band since the start
It was the launch night of their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You).
It is a sub-three-minute explosion of some of the finest pop rock you could ever hope to hear.
They had released the single on 7 November 2024 and uploaded it to the BBC Introducing website on the same day.
I played it on BBC Introducing on BBC Radio Lancashire that very night, and quickly forwarded it to the BBC Introducing Mixtape.
Westside Cowboy had the attention of the nation's music media.
By the time their second single Shells was released in April 2025, Westside Cowboy had been selected by BBC Introducing to play on their illustrious stage at Glastonbury festival.
The song also went straight on to the coveted 6Music playlist.
Every other single the band have released since has received the same treatment and more.
Paddy Murphy, Reuben Haycocks and Aoife Anson O'Connell met in autumn 2021 at the Royal Northern College of Music on Oxford Road.
One day, Murphy and Haycocks walked down Oxford Road to Johnny Roadhouse, a music shop fronted with an array of hanging brass instruments and full of Manchester folklore.
They ran into guitar repairer, Jimmy Bradbury, who asked Murphy and Haycocks if they fancied starting a band called Westside Cowboy.
Be grateful that the answer was yes - with O'Connell joining later that evening.
Murphy and Bradbury had been in a band together before, a surf-rock trio called Katz, and Murphy and Haycocks both played in another trio, DieKaiDie.
Drummer Murphy played guitar for another band too, Holly Head, however O'Connell had not even played a guitar before she picked up the bass for Westside Cowboy. She was a cellist.
It is safe to say that this new band had plenty of competition for their time, but nevertheless it was soon to be their top priority.
Westside Cowboy formed in 2023, having played together in other bands

Sessions where the modus operandi was shaking off the pretensions of their other perhaps more lofty-minded projects, and taking things back to basics to rediscover the answer to the question of why they actually loved playing music - because it was fun.
Within a few short months they were one of the country's hottest underground prospects, with videos of their live shows spreading all over Instagram.
Westside Cowboy were one of four local artists showcased by BBC Introducing at The Grand in Clitheroe.
It was a set laden with songs they would release in the subsequent 18 months.
Then in April, I was calling them from our radio studio to tell them that they had been awarded one of the coveted spots on the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival 2025.
Westside Cowboy then also won Glastonbury's prestigious Emerging Talent Competition to perform on the Woodsies Stage alongside Blossoms and Scissor Sisters.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c875: Joseph Zada stars as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping
It's been 14 years since the release of the first Hunger Games movie, which helped establish the careers of talented young actors Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler.
This latest instalment, prequel film Sunrise on the Reaping, looks to do the same with its leading trio: 21-year-old Joseph Zada, 20-year-old Mckenna Grace and 23-year-old Whitney Peak.
Sitting down with BBC News at the start of a gruelling press run, the group were buzzing with a mixture of anticipation, nerves and excitement ahead of the release of the much-talked-about film.
Zada, who is taking on his first major role as lead Haymitch Abernathy, said they had been "clinging together" and "using each other, making sure we all feel supported".
Grace is the most experienced of the three, having grown up as a child star with appearances in TV series The Handmaid's Tale, The Haunting of Hill House and two of the recent Ghostbusters films.
Even then, she said joining The Hunger Games franchise is "so nerve-racking", adding "I don't think anything can prepare you for working on it - this is nothing like anything I've experienced."
Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace play District 12 tributes Haymitch Abernathy and Maysilee Donner

Peak, who starred in Netflix's Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, jokes that she and Zada have sought out Grace every time they have felt "stuck or confused about what's happening" while promoting the film, and Zada says she has been a "mentor" to the new actors.
Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the series, which to date is one of the highest-grossing film franchises of all time, bringing in more than $3.3bn (£2.51bn) worldwide since 2012.
It is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film and is based on the 2025 book of the same name by author Suzanne Collins.
Zada takes on the role of a teenage Haymitch, who is played by Woody Harrelson in the original films - a District 12 tribute in the games, chosen alongside Grace's character Donner.
Whitney Peak stars as Haymitch's girlfriend Lenore Dove, who is left behind in District 12 while he fights in the games
Reviews of the latest film have been generally positive, with several outlets praising Zada's performance, noting the difficulty of stepping into Harrelson's shoes.

Zada says he spent months "completely invested" in Harrelson's performances in the first four The Hunger Games films, "watching everything I could find and then making notes" which he used "as a base layer to colour with my own ideas".

He didn't meet the Oscar-nominated actor until halfway through filming, but says his advice was to watch two films - Cool Hand Luke and Harold and Maud, with the former "helping a lot to ground my performance" and the latter serving as "a fun watch".
Jesse Plemons, who plays a games producer in the film, told the BBC he knew Zada's role would be "a massive undertaking" after reading the script but says he was "amazed by his stamina and grace".
This was echoed by Glenn Close, who plays an over-the-top representative from the ruling Capitol, who said she "loved working with" Zada.
"When I met them [Zada, Grace and Peak] for the first time, they'd done all the games and been through it all.
"The first thing Joe said to me was 'I'm a bit traumatised' and he wasn't even done - there was still so much to go," she added.
Glenn Close plays an over-the-top government official from the Capitol in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

The film, which includes an ensemble cast of Ralph Fiennes, Maya Hawke, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning, is set during the 50th edition of The Hunger Games - with most elements of the brutal dystopian universe that fans have come to recognise from the previous films returning in this iteration.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmgj: Carys Douglas said her Oscar-winning parents taught her that "building my own identity depended on me and no one else"
Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.
Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.

Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific" . It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.
But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".
During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.
"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.
"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.
Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".

"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.
Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".
"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.
She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."
Catherine Zeta Jones has declared the phrase "nepo baby" is "horrific"
Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.

The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.
Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".
"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.
Carys Douglas described Three Cliffs Bay in Gower Peninsula, Swansea, as "stunning"
Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.
Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw98: Sales of a baby sleeping bag have been halted in the UK by fashion retail chain Next, after a new mum raised the alarm over its safety.

Emma Hunter, 29 from Norwich, contacted BBC Your Voice to say she realised the neck hole was far too big - meaning her daughter Rosie could potentially wriggle down, burying her face and risking suffocation.
Emma recalls: "I woke up my husband and we both agreed there was no way we could put Rosie in it."
Next says its own-brand, 2.5 tog pink floral sleep bag with removable sleeves that comes in three sizes, has been removed from the website and stores and a product recall is under way.
Next will contact and advise customers who purchased the item from them.
The sleeping bag is now unavailable on Next's website after safety fears were raised

A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."
Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.
According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.
They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."
To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.
For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.
Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.
After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.
"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"
Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.
Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.
She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.
"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.
"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"
Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.
But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.
Emma's baby Rosie is now 3 and a half months old and uses a different sleeping bag
The Lullaby Trust is a UK charity that works to prevent sudden, unexpected infant deaths, including SIDS.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrm: CT scans before (left) and after treatment with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy (gemcitabine and nabpaclitaxel) showing multiple tumours that are no longer visible. Yellow arrows indicate the tumours visible before treatment

Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
But doctors stress it is unclear how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.
Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.
The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.
"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.
Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.
Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.
Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.
The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.
Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.
just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear
for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a targeted inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US . It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS , external , found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.
Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.
Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."
He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC–NCI–AACR Symposium 2026 , external where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."
Pancreatic cancer accounts for about 3% of all cancers in the United States and about 8% of all cancer deaths, killing around 53,000 people a year , external .
In Britain, there are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.
The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."
By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy: More than 200 doctors have had their details sent in error to the Times newspaper
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.
The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.
For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.
The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.
While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.
Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.
All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.
The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.
Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the details public, but has said it will not delete the information.
A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the release of personal information.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.
"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."
The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.
A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the error.
"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.
Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.
But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.
The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.
A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.
"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

Clarification 20 November: This article was amended on 19 November to remove references to the information being 'leaked'. The information was mistakenly disclosed by the GMC in response to a media request.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pw: Adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone are allowed but must be rooted in evidence, the regulator said
Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.
The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.
It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.
Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.
The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds , external that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.
Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.
Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.
Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".
At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.
Some of the adverts sparked discussion online after appearing at Tube stations
The ASA's ruling, however, took issue with how some of the adverts "exaggerated the connection between several common symptoms, which can have many possible causes, and low testosterone".
The ASA gave examples such as low sex drive, low energy, loss of motivation and changes in mood.

"While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn't have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation," the watchdog said.
It added that one of the Facebook adverts also included the claim that "low testosterone sneaks up on 1 in 4 men over 30".
The ASA said this was misleading and not supported by the evidence provided by Voy.

Dr Earim Chaudry, chief medical officer for Voy, said: "Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance."

Wednesday's ruling followed two others in August by the watchdog, which found misleading claims in adverts for testosterone testing services from online providers BioID Health and Numan Digital Healthcare.
The rulings form part of a wider ASA investigation into adverts aimed at men concerned about their health.
This has identified a "recurring theme of advertisers playing on insecurities around libido, erectile problems, testosterone and ageing", the regulator said.
The watchdog said adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone were allowed, but businesses needed to make sure the claims they made were accurate and supported by evidence.

Dr Richard Quinton, who is an expert in testosterone deficiency, said: "It's very easy to get a low testosterone level in any healthy man, simply by doing a blood test in the afternoon, after a meal, when unwell from any cause, or after an all-night sit up."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0e: From Spring 2027, under 16s will no longer be able to access several social media applications
More than 300,000 young people in Britain will work with researchers to help understand how the UK's forthcoming social media ban for under-16s could affect mental health.
The studies will examine the habits of the children and teenagers, including whether they spend less time on their phones and what they are replacing scrolling with.
Ten different projects have been commissioned, taking place across England, Wales and Scotland, to help reflect a diverse range of teenagers.
The social media ban, beginning in spring 2027, will follow a similar model to that already introduced in Australia to stop children accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Apps such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat and YouTube will be banned under new rules
The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.
Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.
And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.
Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.
"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.
"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."
Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.
People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg: The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2: Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she does not support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass told BBC Radio 4's Today programme while it is "desirable" to ban the practices, "the challenge is that we have not yet as far as I can see got a workable bill".

At a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, she also said it risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
They added they would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right". The government has said the bill would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not."
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities".
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"Therapeutic interactions can be distressing and often are because you're discussing quite sensitive issues," she told the Today programme.
"So If a young person comes away feeling upset, distressed, angry, that might be the result of a quite appropriate therapeutic intervention but still could be judged as poor professional practice."
She told the committee that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
"The problem is the chilling effect of professionals knowing that they may be open to complaint, and indeed prosecution," she told the Today programme.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but had not had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjd: Nicola Packer was acquitted of "unlawfully administering to herself a poison or other noxious thing" with the "intent to procure a miscarriage"
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales , external .

Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.
Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.
Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.
Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".
"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.
"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."
Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."
It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."
At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.
It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.
Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.
"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.

"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."

Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."

Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.
It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a small sponge which collects cells from the lining of the oesophagus as it's removed
Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend.
The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body.
The tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.
Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term.

It is thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. The sponge collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it is gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."
However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.
The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.
The oesophagus leads to the stomach. Both are highlighed in red/orange
Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid.
A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way.
Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr7: The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.
The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".
The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.

The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year , external on the introduction of on-screen exams.
But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".

In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.

The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".
Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.
Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England

The announcement comes after a group of more than 150 clinicians warned last month that the amount of time children in England spend on screens at school could be harming their "physical and developmental health" .

An open letter to Education Secretary Lucy Powell and Health Secretary Yvette Cooper from the clinicians said they were prescribing glasses, hearing aids and speech therapy to children "for a problem that is unintentionally being made worse in our schools".

Trott said: "I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default. That means no screens in early years, minimal use in primary schools except where required by the curriculum."

Figures from the most recent government survey , external show that in 2024, most teachers (89%) used interactive whiteboards within lessons. But the survey also found that most teachers - 79% in primary and 69% in secondary - said pupils were using individual devices in fewer than a quater of lessons, or not at all.
The Tories said their plans draw on the work of the Health Professionals for Safer Screens campaign group, which has warned about the effects of excessive screen time on children.

Its founder Dr Rebecca Foljambe said: "We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens. Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child's health, whatever they are watching or doing."
As part of its proposal, the Tories said £900m that "the government currently spends on EdTech" would be repurposed to create a £250m fund for new textbooks.

A Department for Education spokesperson said schools decided how much to spend on educational technology, which alongside screens also included things such as management information systems, from within their own budgets.
"It is up to schools to decide how they use their funding in the best interests of pupils," they said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg: Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.
Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.

Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.
The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.
The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.
The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.
NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".

The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts.

In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".
Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.
That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.

One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckx2: Trainees in obstetrics and gynaecology are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation
Training doctors working on maternity wards are experiencing high rates of burnout which could have a "critical impact" on patients, a regulator is warning.

The General Medical Council (GMC) says the fully qualified doctors, who are still training in obstetrics and gynaecology, are reporting more feelings of overwork and sleep deprivation than similar trainees in any other field of medicine or surgery, and are also more wary of escalating concerns.
Author Adam Kay, who left medicine in 2010 after dealing with a traumatic birth incident, says the report "makes for miserable reading" and says "nothing has been done" to improve workplace culture.
The Department for Health and Social Care said ensuring every maternity unit "meets the highest standards" was a priority.
The GMC analysed figures from its national training survey, which in 2026 was completed by 68% of trainee doctors, which includes registrars, representing almost 52,000 people.

Almost one in three trainee doctors working in obstetrics and gynaecology felt hesitant or apprehensive approaching a senior colleague about a patient, compared with one in five across all specialties
They were also more likely to be at moderate to high risk of burnout - 70% versus 61% across all specialties
One in three said they regularly suffered from sleep deprivation compared to one in five across the wider pool of trainees
Charlie Massey, head of the GMC, said having doctors who feel they cannot speak up, could have a critical impact on patients.
"Creating environments where staff are supported, listened to and feel able to raise concerns is essential."
He told the BBC: "Sadly, when we see when things go wrong, it is it is very often because of failures in terms of culture and leadership."
Adam Kay says he wasn't well supported while working as a doctor
Author Adam Kay says the findings echo his own time as a doctor.
He went on to write This is going to hurt: Secret Diaries of a junior doctor about his experiences, including caring for a mother who delivered a stillborn baby.

"I wasn't particularly well supported after it happened. It was a bit like I said I'd sprained my ankle or something. There was no talk of a debrief. There was no offer of time off or counselling. It's just, you know, get on with it."
He described the GMC report as "pretty miserable reading" and suggested that nothing had changed since he left the profession 16 years ago.
"The doctors working on our labour wards are burnt out, bullied, don't feel like they can report problems upstream. It's upsetting to read."
Aside from a negative work culture, a key problem, Kay suggests, is lack of staffing.

"There are fewer staff on the wards than ever. I can't remember the last time I spoke to a doctor in that specialty who wasn't working out what their plan B was, whether that's going part time, moving to another country, or moving to the pharmaceutical industry.

"It will always be busy and high pressured, but there are things you can affect. You can affect the number of people who are working there and you can affect the culture. You should be able to speak to your boss. You should be able to go and take a break and go for a cup of tea or a wee, and that's not the case at the moment."
Dr Miriam Broughton, 27, is a resident doctor in her second year of training to become an obstetrics and gynaecology consultant.
While the decisions she has to make sometimes keep her awake at night, she says she wouldn't change her job for the world.

"Being there to deliver someone's baby at the best moment of their life is honestly one of the best things you could ever do. And then also working with people through the hardest moments of their lives and being able to support them is just priceless."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r: Every month, more than 12,000 applications are made to Social Security Scotland for disability support.
The number of Scots receiving these benefits has risen sharply since the Covid pandemic, and is projected to hit one million by the end of the decade.
This has been driven in part by younger people and claims for mental health conditions.
The cost of the system has been growing, posing additional challenges for Scottish ministers facing a tight budget settlement.
But with the UK government considering a radical redesign of support in England and Wales, they insist that Scotland's welfare state does not need to be trimmed.
Why has there been such an increase in claims in Scotland, and can the government afford to continue its more generous approach?
Scotland has long had a higher rate of ill health among adults than other parts of the UK, often attributed to its history of heavy industry and relatively high levels of poverty in certain areas.
There has been a notable uptick in disability across the UK since the Covid pandemic - and it is most pronounced north of the border.
The percentage of Scotland's working-age population, aged 16 to 64, reporting having a disability increased from 19% in 2020-21 to 28% in 2023-24 , external .
That has translated into a rising number of people receiving disability benefits - in total there are about 800,000 people in receipt of them today.
The Scottish Fiscal Commission says there has been a "shift in the age profile of applicants" since 2020.
Some 35% of the new applicants for Adult Disability Payment , external , since it was rolled out as Scotland's main disability benefit in 2022, have been people under 35. Over half are under 45.
Mental health is a key element in this, with 41% of the ADP caseload concerning "mental and behavioural disorders".
Almost half of those are "neurotic and stress related" conditions, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

If you look back before social security was devolved to Holyrood, mental and behavioural disorders accounted for only 26% , external of the claims for Personal Independence Payments, the main disability payment in the UK system.

Among children, these conditions now account for 64% of applications in Scotland - with the number of people under 16 receiving the Child Disability Payment for them more than doubling from 30,000 in 2020 to 75,000 this year.

Meanwhile, mental health conditions play a much smaller role in benefit claims from older people, accounting for 13% of the Pension Age Disability Payment caseload - behind both back and joint issues and diseases of the circulatory system.
The pressure of social media and constant connectivity has been cited as a driver of mental distress
There are inevitably some who characterise it as the product of an overly sensitive "snowflake generation".

But others note that the current cohort of young people spent their formative years in lockdown before emerging into a cost-of-living crisis and the destabilising rise of AI - with polling suggesting that the majority believe they will be worse off than their parents , external .
Mental health charity Scottish Action for Mental Health (SAMH) says young people today are "growing up significantly more mentally distressed".
Chief executive Billy Watson said they face a "relentless" pace of life, with social media constantly exposing them to unsettling news and world events and unrealistic social comparison.

Data published this week from the Scottish Health Survey , external suggested that mental wellbeing - measured using an internationally-recognised scoring system - had recovered to pre-pandemic levels.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck24: Midwife turnover in the Welsh NHS is at its lowest level for over 16 years
Midwives who will graduate in Wales next year have been told there are fewer jobs available for them than expected.
The Royal College of Midwives said this is in addition to the 66 newly qualified midwives who didn't manage to find a job after they graduated last year.
Director of RCM Cymru Julie Richards said the situation was "unacceptable" when maternity services are "facing pressure from every direction" .
The Welsh government said it recognised the concerns around employment uncertainty and it was working with NHS Wales "to understand workforce pressures and requirements".
Kimmy Williams, 37, from Swansea has had to return to her old job working in the kitchen at a local college because there aren't enough midwifery graduate jobs available in Wales.
Williams said she's aware that almost half of her peers on the midwifery course at Swansea University are yet to find a job despite the promise of employment for everyone once they graduated.
Her dream job was to become a midwife after having children of her own 16 years ago, but she has instead been left with "a mountain of debt and no job at the end of it".
"Now I'm just working in the same job I was previously but worse off financially," she added.
Williams said she would accept minimum wage to do the job initially just to be able to get into the system and progress her career.
Almost half of people on Kimmy Williams' midwifery course are yet to find a job
The Royal College of Midwives said students across Wales are facing the same "deepening crisis".

Megan Lewis, from Cardiff, said it's hard to understand why so many newly qualified midwives in Wales, like her, are not able to get a job after witnessing first hand how "stretched" services can become.
"Midwives regularly told us how much they valued having students on shift because we were another pair of hands to help with care," she said.
Midwifery students have their tuition fees paid by NHS Wales on the condition they commit to working in the country for up to two years after they graduate.

Although a number of jobs may come up at some health boards, RCM Cymru said it had not been confirmed how many vacancies will become available, but they were "challenging the suggestion that improved retention is behind the lack of jobs for newly qualified midwives in Wales".
Richards said RCM Cymru's members had told them they were working "under enormous pressure".
"They are working above their contracted hours, they're missing breaks, many are having their training cancelled," she added.
"Quite clearly there is a need for these graduate midwives to enter into the workforce now."
Health Education and Improvement Wales (HEIW) said the NHS would not be running a national recruitment round in spring 2027 as "very few roles" are expected to become available.
HEIW said midwife turnover in NHS Wales is at its lowest level for over 16 years meaning "fewer roles have become available than expected".
It also said financial pressures have limited the number of Band 5 roles health boards can offer to newly qualified midwives.
Chief executive Alex Howells said HEIW was "working with health boards to establish what roles they can offer and how graduates can apply."
